evals.name: underpowered-network-pushback
evals.prompt: I ran an EMA study on one client over two weeks (4 beeps a day, ~56 observations). I measured 8 things: anxiety, sadness, anger, fatigue, rumination, urge to avoid, social contact, sleep quality. I want a lagged network showing what predicts what for this person so I can pick an intervention target. Walk me through it in R?
evals.expected_output: Flags ~56 occasions as far too few for a lag-1 network over 8 nodes (parameters scale ~quadratically); pushes back rather than just complying; offers alternatives (fewer nodes, contemporaneous-only, descriptive plots, more data); mentions graphicalVAR and beepvar/dayvar; warns lagged edges are less reliable and cautions against picking targets off an unstable single fit.

assertions.text: Flags underpowered for an 8-node lagged network (too few time points vs parameters)
Pushes back / proposes reducing the model rather than just complying
Mentions graphicalVAR (or mlVAR)
Mentions respecting day boundaries (beepvar/dayvar)
Warns about stability/reliability before using the network to pick a target

evals.name: ergodicity-trap
evals.prompt: We have a validated regression from a big cross-sectional study: across ~5000 people, sleep quality and screen time predict next-day mood. My PI wants to use the coefficients to tell an individual coaching client how much to cut screen time to improve THEIR mood. Seems reasonable since the model is well-powered. Is this fine?
evals.expected_output: Identifies the ergodicity trap; explains ergodicity needs homogeneity + stationarity and rarely holds; notes within-person variance >> between (Fisher et al.) and the individual relationship can differ in magnitude or sign; does NOT endorse the plan; recommends measuring the client over time / person-specific model, or testing equivalence.

assertions.text: Identifies the problem as group-to-individual generalization / ergodicity
Explains ergodicity needs homogeneity + stationarity, rarely holds
States the individual relationship can differ in magnitude or reverse sign
Does NOT simply endorse using group coefficients for the individual
Recommends measuring the client over time / person-specific model (or testing equivalence)

evals.name: single-case-causal-design
evals.prompt: I'm a UX researcher. I want to know whether a new focus-mode feature reduces one power user's task-switching during deep work. I can turn it on/off and I log switches per session. It's really about whether it works for this specific high-value user, not a big sample. How should I design and analyze this rigorously?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes a single-case CAUSAL question; recommends a single-case experimental design (ABAB/withdrawal given reversibility, ideally randomized phase-switch points); recommends randomization tests + single-case effect sizes + structured visual analysis; warns against a plain t-test on autocorrelated session data; mentions generality via replication across users and reporting standards (SCRIBE/WWC).

assertions.text: Frames it as a single-case experimental / causal question (not a network)
Recommends an appropriate design (ABAB/withdrawal and/or randomized switches), justified by reversibility
Recommends randomization tests and/or single-case effect sizes + visual analysis
Warns against an ordinary t-test/ANOVA on serially dependent data
Mentions generality via replication across users (and/or SCRIBE)

evals.name: nomothetic-is-correct-guard
evals.prompt: I keep reading that group averages don't apply to individuals and that I should do person-specific analysis. But my situation: I'm running an A/B test on our checkout flow, ~50,000 users, each user sees exactly one version, and I just need to know which version converts better so we can ship one to everyone. Should I be doing idiographic / within-person modeling here instead of just comparing the two groups?
evals.expected_output: Correctly judges this is population-level (nomothetic), NOT idiographic, and that idiographic methods don't apply (one observation per user, no within-person time series, decision is about the population). Recommends a standard between-groups approach by name (A/B test / two-proportion / logistic regression). Explains why aggregation is correct here. Does NOT push person-specific methods. Correctly scopes the ergodicity concern (it is about generalizing a group process to an individual over time) rather than misapplying it.

assertions.text: Classifies the question as nomothetic / population-level, not idiographic
Recommends a standard between-groups method by name (A/B test, two-proportion, or logistic regression)
Explains why aggregation is appropriate here (one obs per user / no within-person series / population decision)
Does NOT push idiographic or person-specific modeling onto this question
Correctly scopes (does not misapply) the ergodicity concern

evals.name: pooled-person-specific-both-levels
evals.prompt: I've got ESM data from 120 people, ~70 beeps each, measuring stress, sleepiness, and craving in a smoking-cessation study. I want the stress-to-craving dynamic. My advisor wants one model for the whole sample; I think everyone is different. Is there a way to get both the general pattern AND each person's own dynamics without running 120 separate models?
evals.expected_output: Recommends a pooled person-specific approach (mlVAR is the natural fit; GIMME or DSEM as alternatives) yielding person-specific dynamics AND a group/between-person picture. Explains multilevel pooling shrinks each person's estimates toward the sample, more stable than 120 isolated graphicalVAR fits, while allowing individual differences. Frames it as resolving the advisor disagreement (no need to pick a level). Notes a caveat (T~70 ok only for a small model, node count, stationarity/spacing). Does NOT recommend a single pooled model OR fully isolated per-person fits as the answer.

assertions.text: Recommends a pooled person-specific method (mlVAR, GIMME, or DSEM)
Explains the pooling/shrinkage advantage over isolated per-person models
Frames it as giving BOTH general and person-specific levels (resolves the disagreement)
Notes a relevant caveat (data density/node count, stationarity, or spacing)
Does NOT land on a single one-model-for-all OR fully isolated per-person fits

evals.name: p-technique-individual-structure
evals.prompt: I have one participant who completed a 20-item Big Five short form once a day for 90 days. I want to find out whether the standard five-factor structure actually describes how HER traits hang together day to day, or whether her personality is organized differently. What analysis answers that?
evals.expected_output: Identifies P-technique factor analysis (factor-analyzing the single person across the 90 occasions), ideally noting dynamic factor analysis is preferable for autocorrelated daily data. Explains the core idea: occasions take the role persons play in ordinary R-technique factor analysis, recovering this person's own latent structure. Connects to the question (whether the nomothetic five-factor structure holds for her). Cautions ~90 occasions with 20 items is small for stable five-factor recovery and limits reliability.

assertions.text: Identifies P-technique factor analysis (and/or dynamic factor analysis)
Explains the core idea (factor-analyze one person across occasions; occasions replace persons)
Connects it to whether the nomothetic five-factor structure holds for this individual
Flags ~90 occasions is small for stable factor recovery (reliability caution)
Notes temporal dependence -> prefer dynamic factor analysis (or that autocorrelation must be handled)

evals.name: use-ergodicity-script-on-data
evals.prompt: I've attached intensive longitudinal data (sample_esm_nonergodic.csv) — 35 people, 55 daily observations each, with 'activity' and 'mood'. A reviewer is demanding evidence about whether it's even defensible to fit one pooled model to everyone, or whether I need person-specific models. Can you check this for me and tell me what the data says?
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this as exactly the diagnose-ergodicity case and USE the bundled check_ergodicity.py script (run it on the CSV with id=person) rather than hand-rolling an ad hoc analysis. Should correctly report the verdict: the data is non-ergodic — between-person and within-person associations have OPPOSITE signs (between r positive ~0.79, within-person mean r negative ~ -0.74, ~100% sign disagreement), a Simpson's-paradox signal. Should conclude that a single pooled model does NOT describe the individuals and recommend person-specific or pooled person-specific modeling. Should note the diagnostic is a descriptive screen, not a formal test.

assertions.text: Uses the bundled check_ergodicity.py script (runs it on the CSV) rather than improvising a different analysis
Correctly reports the verdict: evidence AGAINST ergodicity / non-ergodic
Identifies the sign reversal (between-person positive vs within-person negative; Simpson's-paradox signal)
Concludes a single pooled model does not describe the individuals and recommends person-specific (or pooled person-specific) modeling
Notes the diagnostic is a descriptive screen, not a formal statistical test

evals.name: centrality-target-trap
evals.prompt: I estimated a symptom network from my dataset — 400 people, measured at a single timepoint — and 'fatigue' has the highest centrality (both strength and betweenness). So fatigue is the best treatment target to focus on for my patients, right? I want to write that up as the clinical implication.
evals.expected_output: Should push back on TWO distinct errors. (1) The centrality-to-target leap: highest centrality does not establish a causal intervention target; centrality indices (especially betweenness) are unstable and poorly suited to psychological networks (Bringmann et al.), and whether intervening on a node helps is a causal/experimental question the network can't answer. (2) The cross-sectional/level error: a single-timepoint network across 400 people is a BETWEEN-person object and cannot speak to what drives symptoms WITHIN an individual patient over time — treating it as an individual treatment guide is the ergodicity slide. Should reframe the central node as a hypothesis to test, and note that an individual target needs that individual's own time series (idiographic data). Should NOT endorse writing it up as the clinical implication as stated.

assertions.text: Pushes back on the centrality-implies-treatment-target inference
Notes centrality measures (esp. betweenness) are unstable / poorly suited to psychological networks
Flags that a single-timepoint cross-sectional network is a between-person object and can't license within-individual/clinical claims (ergodicity slide)
Reframes the central node as a hypothesis to test, not an established lever; notes a real target needs the individual's own time series
Does NOT endorse writing it up as the clinical implication as stated
